appraisal_events.evidence: Swann reports at length the Prince's confession (scruples about the trial's legality, secret reading of l'Aurore, masses said for Dreyfus) and concludes: « ces paroles du prince de Guermantes m'ont profondément ému [...] vous auriez de l'admiration pour lui, et il en mérite. D'ailleurs, son opinion ne m'étonne pas, c'est une nature si droite ! »
appraisal_events.explanation: The dominant movement of the passage is Swann's sympathetic relaying of the Prince's dreyfusard conversion, sealed by explicit, unqualified admiration; the same narrated confession also reveals the Princesse as the earlier and secret dreyfusarde, the « oiseau rare » who turns out to be his own wife.

appraisal_events.evidence: On Charlus, Swann assures the narrator « tenez pour assuré que cela ne s'est jamais passé ailleurs que dans sa tête et dans son cœur », while the narrator has just said « je savais fort bien depuis tantôt que ce que je voulais dire était vrai »; and the closing paragraph: « Swann oubliait que, dans l'après-midi, il m'avait dit au contraire que les opinions en cette affaire Dreyfus étaient commandées par l'atavisme », the credited faculty sliding from atavisme to intelligence to droiture as his conclusion requires.
appraisal_events.explanation: The narrator frames Swann twice as an unreliable judge — mistaken (or complacent) about Charlus, and silently rewriting his own explanatory principle to fit whom he now approves — and generalizes the maneuver as the common motivated reasoning about allies and adversaries.

status_effects.explanation: The long quoted confession presents him as painfully scrupulous and finally just, and Swann declares him deserving of admiration and « une nature si droite ».

The revelation that the other, earlier dreyfusard was « La princesse de Guermantes », who had masses said before her husband had lost his doubts, locally raises her above the movement's own protagonist.

His authority as an interpreter is undercut: the narrator marks his Charlus denial as false and exposes his shifting explanation of dreyfusard conviction, so his verdicts are shown to follow his sympathies.

ambiguities: Whether the narrator endorses Swann's admiration of the Prince: the closing paragraph relativizes Swann's grounds for admiring him (atavisme, then intelligence, then droiture du cœur) without denying the Prince's merit, so E1 is read as reported sympathetically but not narratorially underwritten.

The refused invitation (the duc de Guermantes conveying Oriane's message about Marie and Gilbert's table of five or six) could be read as the narrator's inclusion in a highly valued social space, but the passage records neither pride nor loss and diverts into a general essay on orders of pleasure, so no status movement is recorded for it.
